newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bomb defense kept shifting position in case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bomb defense kept shifting position in case.

text.p: The prosecution had most of the cards and played them masterfully in the Oklahoma City bombing trial, but the defence was let down by a constantly shifting strategy, some legal analysts said on Friday.

A federal jury in Denver handed the prosecution a victory Friday by sentencing Timothy McVeigh to death for blowing up the Oklahoma City federal building, killing 168 people in the worst mass murder in U.S. history.
The same jury found the 29-year-old ex-soldier guilty 11 days ago of the April 19, 1995 bombing, ignoring the defence's insistence that he was innocent.
"From the opening statement on, the prosecution had it all over the defence in terms of advocacy," Denver defence attorney David Japha, who closely followed the trial, said.
"What the prosecution did that was so effective was that they took a lot of information, boiled it down concisely, gave an opening (statement) that was dynamite and stuck to it," he said.
"The defence did not have a coherent theory of the case," Japha said, adding that the defence changed its arguments during the trial.

At first, the defence suggested the real bomber may have died in the blast. During the penalty phase, the defence devoted much of its case to McVeigh's views about the Waco standoff without making clear their significance.

In closing arguments, the defence again shifted ground, seeming to concede McVeigh carried out the bombing. Chief defence attorney Stephen Jones said the jury should spare McVeigh's life because otherwise he would take his secrets about the bombing to the grave.
Acclaimed defence attorney Alan Dershowitz was more outspoken in his criticism of McVeigh's lawyers, saying they presented "an awful, awful defence."
"They gave the jury very little to work with," the Harvard law professor said in a telephone interview with CNN.

Dershowitz said he expected Jones to be fired, perhaps even before an appeal that Jones has said he would file on McVeigh's behalf. He suggested that McVeigh could claim an "ineffective defence of counsel."
Other lawyers rushed to the defence of Jones and his team, saying they did the best they could with the poor hand they were dealt.

Denver trial attorney Scott Robinson said the defence did a very good job. "Jones and his crew should be commended for the courageous job they did in representing one of the most detested defendants in history," he said.

"The prosecution did a superb job, but sometimes it's easy to do a superb job when you have all of the strong evidence, all of the emotion and the resources of the U.S. government to help you," he said.

Robinson said the die was cast for conviction when investigators found a truck axle near the bomb scene that carried the vehicle identification number of the truck rented by McVeigh. "It was a flood of evidence, a flood of emotion...," he said.
Right from the start, the defence was widely seen as having an uphill battle against an overwhelming, although largely circumstantial, government case.

McVeigh was arrested 75 minutes after the bombing with explosives residues on his clothes. An eyewitness identified him as the person who rented the Ryder truck used in the bombing. And, prosecutors said, McVeigh had a motive -- hatred for the U.S. government because of his anger at the 1993 federal siege of the Branch Davidian cult compound at Waco, Texas in which about 80 cult members died.
In the sentencing phase of the trial, the heart-wrenching testimony of dozens of survivors, rescue workers and relatives of bomb victims reduced some of the jurors to tears.

The mitigating circumstances offered by the defence in hopes of saving McVeigh's life paled by comparison. Defence witnesses testified about McVeigh's previous good character and lack of a criminal record.
Even McVeigh defence attorney Rob Nigh said after the trial that the victim impact testimony "was the most painful and emotional thing that I have ever seen."

Nigh said he had no regrets about how McVeigh's defence was handled. "Certainly you think that perhaps strategically you might have done something slightly differently, but I can say without reservation that all of the members of Mr. McVeigh's defence team gave absolutely all they had to...the representation of Mr. McVeigh," he said.
